EMPATHY.whatItMeasures: Empathy and social awareness describe how readily a student notices what other people are feeling and takes it into account. It covers picking up on tone and body language, imagining a situation from someone else's position, and responding to that rather than only to what was said. It is a skill that develops with practice, not a fixed personality trait.
looksLike: Notices when a classmate is upset before being told
Adjusts what they say based on how someone reacts
Considers the other side in a disagreement
Is sought out by friends who need to talk
Uncomfortable when someone is treated unfairly
EMPATHY.learningImplications: Awareness of others supports group work, discussion and any subject involving human behaviour or interpretation. It helps in literature, history and the social sciences, where understanding a perspective is part of the task. In group projects this student often keeps the team functioning. The balance to watch is absorbing other people's stress during high-pressure periods.
development: Setting limits so others' problems are not carried alone
Saying the honest thing as well as the kind thing
Staying steady when others are anxious
Acting on what is noticed rather than only noticing
activities: Practise reflecting back what someone said before replying
Take a mentoring or buddy role with a younger student
Read fiction and discuss why a character acted as they did
Discuss a disagreement from both sides before judging
Volunteer with a community or peer-support activity
EMPATHY.parentTip: Name this as a strength out loud; students who feel deeply are sometimes told they are too sensitive. Help them notice when they are carrying someone else's worry, and that stepping back is allowed. Asking what they think another person was feeling in a situation turns a natural tendency into a deliberate, usable skill.
EMPATHY.studentTip: Reading people is genuinely useful, especially in team work. Two things to practise: acting on what you notice rather than only noticing it, and putting the problem down when it is not yours to carry. Being kind and being honest are not opposites, and the most useful feedback is usually both.

STRESS_MGMT.whatItMeasures: Stress management describes how a student copes when demands rise, such as during exams, deadlines or unexpected change. It covers noticing pressure early, keeping routines going, and using strategies that help rather than ones that simply postpone the problem. This is an educational indicator of coping habits, not a health assessment.
looksLike: Keeps working steadily as deadlines approach
Notices rising pressure before it becomes overwhelming
Has habits that reliably help them settle
Recovers reasonably quickly after a setback
Asks for help when workload becomes unmanageable
STRESS_MGMT.learningImplications: How a student handles pressure strongly affects exam performance, often more than how well they know the content. Steady routines, sleep and planned breaks protect recall. Where coping is still developing, timed practice under mild pressure builds tolerance gradually. The aim is a workable routine before the high-stakes period, not extra effort during it.
development: Preparing earlier so pressure is spread out
Building a reliable wind-down routine
Asking for support before the point of crisis
Separating what can and cannot be controlled
activities: Keep a consistent sleep schedule, especially in exam months
Break large tasks into a written list of small steps
Do timed practice papers to make exam conditions familiar
Build in regular physical activity each week
Agree one person to tell when workload feels unmanageable
STRESS_MGMT.parentTip: During exam periods, protect sleep, meals and some downtime rather than adding study hours; these usually do more for performance than extra revision. Ask how the preparation is going rather than what the predicted marks are. If pressure seems persistently high and is affecting sleep or appetite over weeks, involve the school counsellor.
STRESS_MGMT.studentTip: Most exam stress is reduced by starting earlier, not by working harder later. Break big tasks into small written steps so progress is visible. Practise under timed conditions so the real thing is familiar. Protect sleep, it affects recall more than an extra hour of revision does. Tell someone when it becomes too much.

SELF_MOTIVATION.whatItMeasures: Self-motivation describes how readily a student starts and continues work without being pushed. It covers getting going on something unappealing, keeping effort up when results are slow, and connecting daily work to a goal that matters to them. It tends to vary by subject and situation rather than being fixed.
looksLike: Starts work without repeated reminders
Keeps going when progress is slow
Sets personal goals beyond what is required
Returns to a task after being interrupted
Works from interest rather than only for marks
SELF_MOTIVATION.learningImplications: Self-motivation predicts independent study more than almost any other habit. Where it is strong, the student needs goals rather than supervision. Where it is developing, short tasks with visible completion, and a clear link between today's work and something they care about, tend to work better than longer study targets or pressure.
development: Getting started on unappealing tasks
Keeping momentum without immediate results
Turning long-term goals into weekly actions
Sustaining effort in less interesting subjects
activities: Use a two-minute start rule for tasks you are avoiding
Set one specific weekly goal and tick it off visibly
Track a streak of completed study days
Write down why a subject matters before revising it
Study the least appealing subject first, not last
SELF_MOTIVATION.parentTip: Motivation grows from ownership. Let this student set some of their own goals rather than receiving a timetable, and notice effort and consistency rather than only marks. If a subject has stalled, look for whether it feels pointless to them; explaining what it is actually for often restarts effort faster than pressure does.
SELF_MOTIVATION.studentTip: Waiting to feel like it is the slowest way to start. Agree to work for two minutes and let momentum do the rest. Make progress visible with a checklist or a streak. Do the subject you least want to do first, while your energy is highest, and write one line on why it matters before you start.

RESILIENCE.whatItMeasures: Resilience describes how a student responds to setbacks such as a poor result, a rejection or a plan that did not work. It covers recovering within a reasonable time, treating a failure as information rather than a verdict, and being willing to try again with an adjusted approach. It is built through experience and support rather than being something a student simply has.
looksLike: Recovers within a reasonable time after a poor result
Willing to try again after something did not work
Treats mistakes as information rather than proof of inability
Adjusts approach instead of repeating it
Keeps perspective when one thing goes wrong
RESILIENCE.learningImplications: Resilience determines what happens after a bad test, which over a school career matters more than any single result. A resilient student analyses the paper and changes method; a student still developing this may avoid the subject instead. Reviewing what specifically went wrong, in writing, converts a setback into a plan and is the most reliable way to build this.
development: Separating one result from overall ability
Reviewing a setback instead of avoiding the subject
Asking for help after something goes wrong
Being as fair to yourself as to a friend
activities: After every test, write what went wrong and one change
Keep an error log and revisit it before the next assessment
Set a goal that requires several attempts to reach
Practise a skill where early failure is normal and expected
Talk through a setback with someone before deciding what it means
RESILIENCE.parentTip: How a poor result is handled at home teaches more than the result itself. Ask what they think went wrong and what they would change, before discussing marks. Share your own setbacks and what you did next. If one bad result is treated as a catastrophe, avoidance of that subject usually follows.
RESILIENCE.studentTip: A bad result is data about your method, not a verdict on your ability. Within a day or two, write down exactly what went wrong and the one thing you will change. Then go back to that subject rather than avoiding it, because avoidance is what turns a single bad mark into a long-term weakness.

RESPONSE_CTRL.whatItMeasures: Response control describes the gap a student can create between feeling something and acting on it. It covers pausing before replying when annoyed, thinking through a consequence before speaking, and choosing a response rather than reacting automatically. It develops considerably through adolescence and improves with deliberate practice.
looksLike: Pauses before responding when provoked
Thinks about consequences before speaking
Can hold back a first reaction and choose a better one
Stays measured in disagreements
Recovers composure quickly after being upset
RESPONSE_CTRL.learningImplications: Response control supports classroom relationships and group work, and it matters in exams too: the ability to pause rather than panic when a question looks unfamiliar protects performance. Students still developing this benefit from an agreed, concrete pause strategy rather than being told to calm down, since a specific routine is something they can actually execute.
development: Building a pause before reacting
Noticing early signs of frustration
Expressing disagreement without escalating
Returning to a task after being upset
activities: Practise a count-to-five pause before replying when annoyed
Write a response first and send it later, if at all
Notice and name the physical signs of rising frustration
Role-play a difficult conversation before having it
Use a fixed routine when an exam question looks unfamiliar
RESPONSE_CTRL.parentTip: Model the pause yourself, since this is learned largely by copying. Discuss incidents once everyone is calm rather than in the moment. Agree a specific strategy in advance, such as leaving the room briefly, so there is something concrete to do. Recognise improvement, because progress here is gradual and easy to overlook.
RESPONSE_CTRL.studentTip: The gap between feeling and acting is a skill you can train. Agree one concrete pause with yourself, counting to five, or writing the message without sending it. Learn your own early warning signs so you can act before the reaction, not after. This matters in exams too: a fixed routine beats panic when a question looks strange.

IMPULSE_CTRL.whatItMeasures: Impulse control and thoughtful communication describe how well a student resists acting on the first idea and instead considers before committing. It covers waiting rather than interrupting, checking work before submitting, and thinking about how a message will be received. It is closely tied to planning and to finishing work carefully.
looksLike: Waits for their turn rather than interrupting
Checks work before handing it in
Thinks about how a message will be read
Resists the distraction of the phone during study
Plans before starting rather than diving in
IMPULSE_CTRL.learningImplications: This affects accuracy directly. Many lost marks come from answering too quickly, misreading a question, or not checking. Building a fixed review step into every piece of work usually recovers those marks. It also affects study conditions, since resisting distraction is what makes a study hour worth an hour rather than twenty minutes.
development: Reading the whole question before answering
Building a checking step into every submission
Managing phone and notification distraction
Pausing before sending a message written in frustration
activities: Reserve the last five minutes of any test for checking
Underline what a question actually asks before answering
Study with the phone in another room
Write a plan of two lines before starting a long answer
Wait an hour before replying to anything that annoyed you
IMPULSE_CTRL.parentTip: Focus on process rather than speed. Ask whether the work was checked before it was handed in, and treat careless-error marks as a fixable habit rather than a lack of ability. Agree phone rules for study time together instead of imposing them, since agreed rules are far more likely to survive contact with a difficult evening.
IMPULSE_CTRL.studentTip: A large share of lost marks are not knowledge gaps, they are speed. Underline what the question actually asks, and always keep the last five minutes for checking. Put your phone in another room while studying; willpower is not the tool for that job. Before sending a message written in irritation, wait an hour.

ANGER_MGMT.whatItMeasures: Self-regulation in the context of anger describes how a student handles frustration and irritation. It covers noticing annoyance early, expressing it in a way that does not damage a relationship, and settling afterwards. Frustration itself is normal and useful information; this indicator is about what a student does with it.
looksLike: Notices frustration building before it takes over
Says what is wrong instead of shutting down or lashing out
Settles reasonably quickly after being annoyed
Keeps disagreements about the issue, not the person
Can return to work after an upset
ANGER_MGMT.learningImplications: Frustration tolerance matters most with difficult material. A student who can stay with a problem that is not working learns more than one who abandons it at the first block. Where this is developing, agreeing in advance what to do when stuck, such as attempt twice, then ask, prevents frustration from ending the study session.
development: Naming frustration early rather than holding it in
Having a plan for when work is not going well
Separating the problem from the person
Returning to a task after walking away
activities: Agree a rule: try twice, then ask for help
Take a five-minute break when stuck rather than pushing through
Name what is annoying you in one sentence before reacting
Use physical activity as a regular outlet
Review afterwards what would have helped earlier
ANGER_MGMT.parentTip: Treat frustration as information rather than misbehaviour, and respond to what caused it once things are calm. Avoid discussing an incident while it is still hot. Agree in advance what they can do when stuck on homework, since most study-time frustration comes from being blocked with no agreed way out.
ANGER_MGMT.studentTip: Frustration usually means you are stuck, not that you cannot do it. Agree a rule with yourself: try twice, take a short break, then ask. Naming what is annoying you in a single sentence takes most of the heat out of it. Keep disagreements about the problem rather than about the person.

CONFLICT_CTRL.whatItMeasures: Emotional regulation during conflict describes how a student behaves when there is genuine disagreement. It covers staying in the conversation rather than withdrawing or escalating, listening to a position they disagree with, and looking for a resolution rather than a win. It is a learnable skill that matters in group work and later in almost every workplace.
looksLike: Stays in the conversation during disagreement
Listens to a view they do not share
Looks for a resolution rather than winning
Keeps criticism about the issue, not the person
Can apologise or concede a point
CONFLICT_CTRL.learningImplications: Group projects are where this shows up at school. A student who can handle disagreement keeps a team productive; one who avoids it may agree publicly and disengage privately. Practising structured disagreement, such as stating the other position before your own, builds the skill in a low-stakes setting.
development: Raising a problem instead of avoiding it
Staying calm when strongly disagreeing
Not agreeing publicly while disengaging privately
Separating disagreement from personal criticism
activities: State the other person's position before giving your own
Take part in structured debate, arguing the side you oppose
Raise one small issue early rather than letting it build
Agree group-project roles in writing at the start
Practise conceding a point when the other side is right
CONFLICT_CTRL.parentTip: Let disagreement happen at home in a manageable form; a student who is never allowed to disagree does not learn how to do it well. Model conceding a point when you are wrong. In group-project complaints, help them work out how to raise the issue with the group rather than solving it for them.
CONFLICT_CTRL.studentTip: Disagreement handled well is a serious advantage, especially in group work. Try stating the other person's position first, in their terms, before you give yours; it changes the tone of most arguments. Raise small problems early. Being able to say you were wrong costs nothing and makes people trust your judgement more.

RELATIONSHIP_MGMT.whatItMeasures: Accountability and relationship management describe how a student maintains working relationships over time: keeping commitments, doing their share, repairing things after a disagreement, and being someone others can rely on. It is about consistency and follow-through rather than about popularity.
looksLike: Does their share of group work without chasing
Keeps commitments made to friends and teachers
Repairs a relationship after a disagreement
Admits their part when something goes wrong
Is trusted by others to follow through
RELATIONSHIP_MGMT.learningImplications: Reliability shapes how much responsibility a student is given, which in turn shapes their opportunities. In group projects, a student who does their part on time raises everyone's outcome. Agreeing written roles and deadlines at the start of group work makes accountability concrete rather than a matter of goodwill.
development: Committing only to what can be delivered
Repairing relationships rather than letting them lapse
Raising problems with the person concerned
Balancing others' expectations with own workload
activities: Write down group-project roles and deadlines at the start
Say no clearly when you cannot deliver, rather than going quiet
Follow up once on any commitment you made this week
Apologise specifically rather than generally after a mistake
Check in with a friend you have not spoken to for a while
RELATIONSHIP_MGMT.parentTip: Let this student carry real commitments and experience the consequences when something is not delivered; this is how reliability is learned. Notice and name follow-through when it happens. Encourage repairing a fallen-out friendship rather than simply moving on, since that skill matters well beyond school.
RELATIONSHIP_MGMT.studentTip: Being reliable is quietly one of the most valuable things about you, and it is what gets you trusted with better opportunities. Only commit to what you can actually deliver, and say so clearly when you cannot rather than going silent. After a mistake, apologise for the specific thing; general apologies do not repair much.

ENCOURAGEMENT.whatItMeasures: Social skill in encouraging others describes how a student supports the people around them: noticing effort, giving credit, helping someone who is struggling, and lifting a group's mood. It is a leadership behaviour that does not require a leadership title, and it strongly affects how teams function.
looksLike: Notices and mentions other people's effort
Helps a struggling classmate without being asked
Gives credit rather than taking it
Lifts the mood of a group
Includes people who are on the edge of a group
ENCOURAGEMENT.learningImplications: Encouraging others improves group work and, usefully, the student's own learning: explaining and supporting a classmate consolidates the material. It also builds the social capital that makes study groups and peer help available when they themselves need it. The balance to watch is spending so long supporting others that their own work is squeezed.
development: Balancing support for others with own preparation
Giving honest as well as positive feedback
Accepting encouragement from others
Encouraging specifically rather than generally
activities: Give one specific piece of praise each day, naming what was good
Take a peer-support or buddy role formally
Invite the quietest person in a group to contribute
Practise pairing a positive comment with one honest suggestion
Ask for feedback on your own work as well as giving it
ENCOURAGEMENT.parentTip: Name this strength; encouraging others is a genuine leadership quality that report cards rarely mention. Make sure supporting friends is not consistently eating into their own study time. Encourage the harder half of the skill too, which is being honest as well as positive, since real support sometimes means saying the difficult thing.
ENCOURAGEMENT.studentTip: Encouraging people is a leadership skill, whether or not you hold a title. Make it specific: naming exactly what someone did well is worth far more than a general compliment. Two things to work on, pairing honesty with encouragement, and protecting your own preparation time so supporting others does not quietly cost you your week.

FEEDBACK_ACCEPT.whatItMeasures: Self-awareness and feedback acceptance describe how a student receives correction and uses it. It covers listening without becoming defensive, separating criticism of work from criticism of self, and actually changing something afterwards. It is one of the strongest predictors of improvement over time, because it determines whether teaching turns into progress.
looksLike: Listens to correction without becoming defensive
Asks what specifically to improve
Changes approach after feedback
Separates comments on work from their worth as a person
Seeks out feedback rather than avoiding it
FEEDBACK_ACCEPT.learningImplications: This is the mechanism by which teaching becomes improvement. A student who reads the comments and acts on them gains far more from the same marked paper than one who looks only at the score. Building a habit of turning each piece of feedback into one specific action makes the effect concrete and visible.
development: Hearing criticism without taking it personally
Asking for feedback before the final attempt
Acting on feedback rather than only noting it
Seeking out views that differ from your own
activities: Read the comments on a marked paper before the mark
Turn each piece of feedback into one specific action
Ask a teacher what one change would improve your work most
Show work in draft rather than only when finished
Keep a list of repeated feedback and check it before submitting
careerConnections: Any professional role with review or appraisal
Design and creative work with client revision
FEEDBACK_ACCEPT.parentTip: Separate the work from the child in how you talk about results, since that is what makes feedback bearable. Ask what the teacher suggested rather than only what the mark was. Model it yourself by accepting correction visibly. A student who can hear feedback improves faster than one who is simply told they are clever.
FEEDBACK_ACCEPT.studentTip: Feedback is the cheapest way to improve, so go looking for it rather than waiting. Read the comments before the mark. Turn each comment into one specific thing you will do differently, otherwise it stays an opinion rather than a change. Show work in draft, when there is still time to act on what you hear.
